prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators, and its first experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells

statement.case_for: After the full first round I keep a single-topic prize on topological insulators, with Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, and I no longer treat IceCube as a live part of my configuration. The scientific arc is the cleanest on the shortlist: a sharp prediction (a Z2 invariant that forces protected edge states), a decisive experimental test in HgTe in 2007 that could have failed, and fifteen years of independent confirmation by transport, ARPES and STM, with a concept that has moved into photonics, cold atoms and mechanics. This is nature answering a theoretical question, which is what I look for. Eriksson and Olsson convinced me that the discovery with a clear before and after is the quantum spin Hall effect, not the 3D follow-on, so I keep Mele with Kane and do not substitute Hasan. The citation names the effect and the HgTe observation explicitly so that the prize is for the discovery and not for a vague topic, and it is distinguishable from the 2016 prize on topological phases of matter in one-dimensional chains and the Kosterlitz-Thouless transition: that prize concerned topological order and phase transitions in model systems, whereas this one is about a protected state of real materials with a measurable edge conductance.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weak point and I will not pretend it has been solved. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe as the platform and Molenkamp's experiment tested their prediction, yet none of them can be credited within three names (Zhang is also deceased). Hasan's ARPES observation of the 3D topological insulator and the Fu, Kane and Moore theory are left out of the citation. A sceptic can also call this a second topology prize after 2016, and practical consequences are still modest. If the committee finds that no trio can be defended, then I would rather turn to B001, where the credit is the cleanest on the list, than to a configuration I cannot justify.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice clock is an observation of nature as much as an instrument, since it measures redshift over millimetres and tests constancy of constants, and that nature-driven should not outrank instrument-driven.
responses.response: I accept the correction: I overstated the distinction in round 1, and a measurement that decides a question about nature is a clue from nature. The remaining issue is distinctness, not kind. The lattice clock did show something specific that neither the comb nor the ion clock showed: with the magic wavelength the light shift cancels while thousands of atoms are probed, so ion-level systematic control is combined with a many-atom statistical advantage, and many laboratories now agree at 1e-18. That sentence is enough for me to treat B001 as a distinct discovery, not a refinement, and I move it up to my first alternative. I still weigh it just below topological insulators, because the case that a new concept was tested and confirmed is, to me, clearer there, and because the redefinition of the second has not happened. I will not obstruct B001 on scientific grounds.

responses.point: Eriksson asked why I weigh Hasan's 3D ARPES work above the original Kane-Mele theory pair and argued that leaving out Mele is harder to defend than leaving out the 3D step.
responses.response: I weigh it the other way now. In round 1 I only raised Hasan as a possibility, and your argument persuades me: the discovery with a clean before and after is the quantum spin Hall effect, and Mele shared the founding papers and the invariant from the start. The 3D observation generalises it and is the cost I would accept and state openly. I therefore keep Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. Your point that the citation must separate this clearly from the 2016 prize is taken: I have written it around the protected edge channels of the quantum spin Hall effect observed in HgTe, not the general topological theme.

responses.point: Johansson prefers Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan so that the 3D observation by ARPES is recognised, and asks whether a quantum spin Hall prize leaves it unrecognised at an acceptable cost.
responses.response: I understand the argument that Hasan would otherwise be unrecognised, but I do not think it justifies removing Mele. Hasan's work followed a theory by Fu and Kane and Moore and Balents, so crediting him pulls the citation towards a 3D story whose theory attribution is itself crowded, while removing Mele leaves the founding Kane-Mele paper without one of its authors. The three-name limit forces an omission either way, and I prefer the one that costs the least on the original idea. I would be willing to support a trio with Hasan if the committee decides that way, since I regard both as defensible, but my own vote follows Mele.

responses.point: Pearce asks what I would do about IceCube if not a single name for Halzen, and says the choice is one name following the concept and construction of the detector or no IceCube prize.
responses.response: My answer is no IceCube prize this year in my own configuration. I still value the diffuse flux and the 2018 coincidence, but a single name for a collaboration with AMANDA and DUMAND predecessors is not something I can defend, and I cannot find a defensible three-name list from the shortlist. I would not add names just to fill the slots. I also would not support pairing it with B024 or B001, since that would give B024 only one name or mix the credit problem into a clean case. IceCube stays on my alternatives only if the committee found a credit solution that I cannot see now.

responses.point: Olsson says that the experimental share must carry weight in the B024 citation and that a theory-only prize is unacceptable, since graphene failed and the effect was first seen in HgTe after a different proposal.
responses.response: I agree and it is why Molenkamp is in the configuration and why the citation names the HgTe observation. Your point also helps with the BHZ difficulty, since the experimental verification is what turned a prediction into a discovery. I also agree with the four-way split with Hasan being unattractive and would not go beyond three names.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can accept the omission of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (and of Hasan and Fu, Moore and Balents) as a reasonable cost of a three-name limit.
Whether the 2016 topological-phases prize makes the citation look repetitive, even with the distinction I draw.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second will in a few years make B001 the more natural choice.
Whether Mele or Hasan is the more defensible third name alongside Kane and Molenkamp; I judge Mele, but I hold that view with moderate confidence.
statement.conflict_note: No change to my disclosure. I have no collaboration or institutional link to Kane, Mele, Molenkamp or any other credited name on the shortlist. My PhD supervisor David Gross and my co-author Thomas Van Riet are not on any shortlisted ballot. I note the chair's and others' disclosed proximity to B001, B029 and B021 and discount nothing on my side because of it.
